drapeaux.note: Editorial summary of Articles 7(1) and 10(1), translated from the French; not a quotation. Official English text seen at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/1996/9 (Directive as adopted, Official Journal): Article 7(1) speaks of “a substantial investment in either the obtaining, verification or presentation of the contents”; Article 10(1) says the right “shall expire fifteen years from the first of January of the year following the date of completion” (the summary says, more simply, fifteen years from completion).

The phrase “may consist in the deployment of financial resources and/or the expending of time, effort and energy” is recital 40 of Directive 96/9/EC; checked word for word at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/1996/9 (Directive as adopted) and in the Commission text reproduced at https://cyber.harvard.edu/property00/alternatives/directive.html. EUR-Lex itself could not be opened by an automated client.

The French says the Directive came five years after Feist and “one year after the European Commission formulated its proposal”. The Commission proposal was published in 1992 (OJ C 156, 23.6.1992, cited in the Directive's own footnotes at https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/1996/9), about four years before the adoption of March 11, 1996, not one. Perhaps the intended point is that the proposal came one year after Feist. English kept faithful to the French.

titre: Europe Invents a Right America Had Refused
accroche: In 1996, the European Union creates an entirely new right to protect what an American court had refused five years earlier.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1991, the Supreme Court of the United States rules, in Feist Publications v. Rural Telephone Service, that a telephone directory arranged in alphabetical order deserves no copyright: arranging it requires no creative choice, and the labor invested in gathering the names and numbers changes nothing. A telephone operator can see its directory copied in full by a competitor with no recourse, whatever it cost to compile. The decision settles the American case, but leaves open, on both sides of the Atlantic, the same question: what to do with a database that is costly to build but devoid of any originality?

## A right that protects money, not invention

On March 11, 1996, the European Parliament and the Council adopt Directive 96/9/EC on the legal protection of databases. The text layers two distinct regimes. The first follows the logic of Feist: a classic copyright protects a database's structure, but only if the selection or arrangement of its contents constitutes an original intellectual creation. The second regime, a new one, is a so-called “sui generis” (a right of its own kind) right, granted to the maker of the database: the maker may prohibit the extraction or reutilization of a substantial part of the contents provided that obtaining, verifying or presenting those contents required a substantial investment, financial or human. The text puts it this way: this investment “may consist in the deployment of financial resources and/or the expending of time, effort and energy.” This right lasts fifteen years from the completion of the database, renewable if a new substantial investment changes the contents.

The distinction is clear-cut: where Feist demands a minimum of creativity for any protection, the European sui generis right dispenses with it entirely. It rewards neither an idea nor a composition, only an expense, financial or human, of gathering and maintaining data.

## Two answers to the same question

Five years after Feist, one year after the European Commission formulated its proposal for a directive, jurists of the time read in this timeline the European answer to the legal void the American ruling had just created for costly but non-creative compilations. The connection remains a reading, never stated as such in the text of the Directive itself, but the coincidence of dates and the reciprocity clause it adds, denying the benefit of the sui generis right to producers from countries that offer no comparable protection, make it hard to dismiss.

A telephone directory would therefore meet a different fate depending on whether it is copied in Wichita or in Wiesbaden: free of rights in one case, protected for fifteen years in the other, not because the two systems would judge its creative value differently, both finding it nil, but because they do not seek to reward the same thing.

repere.texte: The sui generis right created in 1996 protects the maker of a database for fifteen years from the completion of the database, on the sole condition of a substantial investment in the obtaining, verification or presentation of its contents, without requiring the slightest ounce of creativity.

carte.punch: The same database is free of rights in the United States and protected for fifteen years in Europe.
carte.idee: In 1996, five years after an American court rules that a telephone directory deserves no copyright, the European Union creates an entirely new right: protecting not the creativity of a database anymore, but the investment needed to build it.

quiz.question: What distinguishes the sui generis right created by the 1996 directive from classic copyright?
choix: It requires an even higher degree of creativity than copyright
It protects substantial investment in a database, without requiring the slightest creativity
It applies only to databases published outside the European Union
It entirely replaces copyright for all digital works
quiz.explication: The sui generis right rewards a substantial financial or human investment in obtaining, verifying or presenting the contents, without requiring creativity: unlike copyright, which remains reserved for the database's original structure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the Supreme Court of the United States rule in Feist in 1991, the origin of the contrast this entry draws?
choix: That a telephone directory arranged alphabetically deserves no copyright, for lack of creativity
That every telephone directory is automatically protected for fifteen years
That only digital databases can be protected, not printed directories
That copyright now protects investment as much as creativity
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Supreme Court rules that an alphabetical arrangement of data that were not invented reflects no creative choice and therefore deserves no copyright protection, whatever the work invested in compiling it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How long does the sui generis right created by Directive 96/9/EC last?
choix: Five years, like a provisional patent
Fifteen years from the completion of the database, renewable in case of a new substantial investment
The entire lifetime of the database's maker
No fixed term: the right lapses upon the first authorized extraction
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Article 10 of the Directive sets the term of the sui generis right at fifteen years from the completion of the database, renewable if a new substantial investment changes its contents.
